title: Playing with Oliver's Chicago band and Carroll Dickerson at the Sunset
summary: Armstrong credits his career to playing with good musicians, names the lineup in Chicago, the Dickerson orchestra at the Sunset, the Charleston era and the finale routine.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: working with men that are better than you and I guess there was a time when there was someone better than you when you were awfully young.

All of my life in music and whatever happened to me right today comes from observing some of the musicians that were playing something. And I was always lucky to play with good musicians. When I went into Chicago I was sitting with Joe, Johnny Dots, Baby Dots and all of them good. Leo on piano and Joe Arroyo and Lauren at Horn. I said, why didn't we do it? Now, I went into the front set with Carol Dickerson's orchestra which was owned by Joe Glazer, my manager, and Joe Glazer and Joe Rollins who was called the Plantation. Well, growing up now, see, now it's a picture, either go back to Jill's band or come over across the street. So your wife could look out for a lot of things in your favor. Say, well, what good is you to go back to play second trumpet with Joe Arroyo, with Carol Dickerson who wants you to play voice trumpet over here? You know what I mean? Yeah. So that's how my popularity comes to get along because the people comes to play that door out for a nun. See, and all the musicians in town would come there in the sunset. And that's when the Charleston was raging. And I was to do so bad, ham up dancing, and I was pat. So they made the finale. One fat one, real high and skinny. Brother Bobby Hall, the drummer man, and Wilson, the drummer player. And we'd bring up that finale and break up the house. See, and he was, I'm tired of playing Four Little Rich Clown. Do you think you played differently for other musicians than you played for a regular rock? Well, we all played the same. I mean, we don't think the same. The regular guys say, well, how did you do when you, what would you think about when you played this riff, that riff? I said, no, I'm not going to get the same when it's long there.
